doc.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023

title: Innovation, finding your voice and starting the trumpet in 1974
summary: Rowe asks about innovation; Vega says he is derivative of his heroes, wanted to play alto sax but started trumpet in January 1974, and values tenor players.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: What is it — you know Phil Woods said that he didn’t consider himself an innovator, he was a craftsman. And maybe — I don’t know how you look at your own playing but does it get harder as time goes by to become an innovator? To come up with something that’s new?

Something that’s completely new? It’s really difficult. We’re in the age of — we’re in the information age on a different level. So there’s so many different things being thrown at us. How does one become an innovator? Well I would say learn as much of the history and gather from it and try to develop your own voice. At this point, like myself as an instrumentalist I just want to be able to tell the story. Hopefully I have my own sound. I’m very derivative of a lot of older people that came before me and I would say so. I mean yeah. I mean there’s some things that I do definitely do that I’ve heard some other younger cats doing as well and I go oh okay, I think you’ve been listening to some of my records but I wouldn’t call myself an innovator by any stretch of the imagination. I just think of myself as a person who wants to be able to play in a fashion that would be respectful to the people that I hold dear to this music — the Freddies, the Woodys, the Dizzys, the James Moodys, James Spaulding. These are people that I came into contact with. I mean I wasn’t dear friends with Woody or Freddie but I had some funny Freddy

stories which I can’t share here because there’s too much foul language in it. But it’s all good — and it was all very positive stuff. But I take in whatever those people did and the things that I love from recordings by people like Donald Byrd and Art Farmer. And then of course I never really wanted to play trumpet. I wanted to play alto saxophone. And they didn’t have them at the middle school — at the — well junior high school is what we called it back then. They didn’t have them. They didn’t have them. I started six months too late so instead of starting in September I started in the band program in January of 1974 so we’re going on to fifty years of me trying to play the trumpet — coming up right now when this January comes up God willing. But all of this to say, I have a close affinity with saxophonists, especially tenor players. Now I just love the sound of that instrument, I love the voice out of it. So there’s a lot of that in my head too just from all the tenor players that I’ve listened to. But I just think it’s important to come from a place of immersing yourself in the sound and hoping to create a statement. If it’s innovative fine. If it’s not innovative and it’s — how shall I say — it sounds as if it’s coming out of a lot of different people that’s okay too. It takes a long time to be able to develop kind of whatever you feel most comfortable with. You know I’m not one that likes to play things at super fast tempos.
